Multi-phonon physics, an emerging domain, functions as a trial ground for fundamental quantum theories with diverse applications in metrology and on-chip communication. Researchers utilize these quantum acoustic cables, bounded within a semiconductor quantum dot by phonons emitted from a stimulated light field, as a probe. Research focuses on using dark-state excitation, distinguished by its robustness against decoherence comparable to that of superconducting circuits or photons, as an input state for multi-phonon systems. However, achieving optical detection is complicated by the intrinsic invisibility of dark excitations to standard luminescence techniques. In this paper, we demonstrate the capability of using optically driven, multi-phonon interactions mediated by dark-state transitions, detected via non-resolving sidebands, to overcome these limitations. We investigate the spectral properties of a low-symmetry 2D electronic lattice: a herringbone system within a non-symmorphic wallpaper group defined by orthogonal glide symmetries along two sets of directions. Diverse functional optimization problems involving system identification, design, estimation, and control are often defined by differential equality and inequality constraints characterized by their infinite-dimensional nature, usually lacking an explicit analytical solution. To address such constrained optimization problems, we employ population-based metaheuristics—including genetic algorithms, particle swarm, and differential evolution—in conjunction with discrete time-collocation techniques for continuous variables. We further ensure convergence by verifying a discrete approximation that remains faithful to the continuous formulation. Evaluation against five benchmark examples reveals that these approaches can reliably locate discrete approximations within acceptable errors. Notably, our framework successfully resolves several unprecedented challenges with high confidence. Additionally, we demonstrate the flexibility of this framework by implementing it on complex, real-world industrial benchmarks with success.

Delineating esophageal tumors in CT scans presents a dual challenge for manual and automatic segmentation: the low tissue contrast near the malignancies, the variable anatomy of the esophagus, and the occasional obscuring effect of foreign bodies like feeding tubes. Consequently, physicians often rely on supplementary data from endoscopy, electronic medical history, and alternative imaging modalities such as PET scans to inform segmentation tasks. However, integrating this extra knowledge is frequently labor-intensive; moreover, the process itself remains error-prone and subject to variability in outcomes. This study aims to evaluate whether and to what degree a streamlined clinical workflow restricted to solely CT data enables the automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors with adequate accuracy. To address this, the authors introduce a fully autonomous segmentation methodology that leverages an end-to-end deep learning architecture utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks. This specific framework was designated the "Fully Unet with Dense Convolution" network (DDAUnet). It integrates spatial and channel gates—also known as Dilatation Unet with Dense Convolution (DDAUnets)—to selectively enhance the network's concentration on critical regions and visual patterns associated with tumors. Furthermore, dilated convolution blocks facilitate model performance and efficiency. This study analyzes 452 high-resolution, multi-modal brain images to evaluate how effectively this approach works with brain tumos segmentation using dilated convolution blocks and channel gates.

Offshore drilling incurs significant expenses, particularly when hydrocarbons exist in complex reservoirs. To maximize production and control these costs from such challenging formations, real-time optimized well placement, known as geosteering, is essential. This process is typically supported by dynamic formation evaluations facilitated by well-log interpretation during drilling. However, this application demands a workflow for interpreting well logs in real-time that is robust, reliable, and computationally efficient while also accounting for various uncertainties. This study integrates an iterative ensemble technique, specifically the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood using approximate Levenberg–Marquardt (LM–EnRML), into the evaluation workflow. By minimizing the statistical discrepancy between observed well log data and theoretical simulations from forward tools, we estimate petrophysical parameters (such as resistivity and density) and layer boundaries along with their associated uncertainties. Synthetic case studies featuring various log types validated the method's ability to accurately forecast model parameters. Comparative CPU time analysis reveals that the proposed approach requires 10–125 times less computational effort per an established method (with a specific implementation of which is not fully detailed). Additionally, the method accurately identifies sand boundaries using model realizations that converge quickly. These findings confirm the method can accurately evaluate formations while ensuring every calculated parameter remains reliable.

Named entity recognition (NER) stands as a pivotal task in natural language processing and core technique for knowledge extraction, extensively utilized to derive information from texts for subsequent applications. Nested NER, a sub-variant of NER, aims at identifying named entities where one entity is completely embedded within another. However, numerous prior studies model these inherently hierarchical nested entities using an inadequate linear structure. To rectify this structural disparity, the current approach models all nested named entities within a sentence as an integral holistic structure, introducing a corresponding parsing algorithm. Additionally, addressing the current absence of corpus-level context in such research is a key contribution. To this end, the work incorporates Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI) and other correlations derived from corpus-wide statistics, thereby enhancing overall performance by extending modeling beyond the sentence level. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed model attains state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance using standard benchmark datasets. Subsequent empirical analyses further indicate that corpus-based features drastically boost performance during domain adaptation.

Tantalum oxides (Ta$_2$O$_5$) exhibit favorable physical and chemical traits, including strong antireflective capabilities and high dielectric constants. In addition, recent studies suggest that Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles could enhance biological efficacy in cancer hadron therapy, and first-principles simulations offer a robust way to study their electronic properties. However, the multiplicity of stable polymorphs poses a significant obstacle to clearly separating their distinct spectral features. To address this challenge, we employed linear-response time-dependent density functional theory to analyze the material-specific energy loss function $\operatorname{Im} (-1/\bar{\epsilon})$ and the metal-dielectric response term $\operatorname{Im} (-\bar{\epsilon})$ for various polymorphs. Our results indicate that characteristic patterns within the loss function of the $\epsilon$ and $(1+\bar{\epsilon})^{-1}$ present reliable signatures for distinguishing structural variants; consequently, these distinct responses enable the accurate prediction of optical and electronic characteristics unique to each polymorph.

Previous studies primarily ascribed the spread of online misinformation to individual traits, such as information literacy, and technological influences like algorithmic distribution, largely overlooking how place-based context shapes these processes. This paper investigates whether and how place context influences misinformation circulation by examining offline personality characteristics and their interaction with the "Echo Location" news consumption habit (defined as preferring politically like-minded sources). Analyzing retweeting behaviors regarding misinformation vaccines myths by over 36,000 U.S. Twitter users during the early pandemic, the findings indicate that in both low- and high-context locations, higher scores of conscientiousness correlate with lower misinformation engagement. Additionally, while conscientiousness consistently suppresses sharing among non-partisans and Democrats, for Republicans and independents, its impact is moderated by context severity: it reduces sharing significantly in low-context areas but loses statistical significance in high-context ones. Consequently, this research suggests that the influence of personality on misinformation dissemination is place-dependent, supporting the conclusion that both context and individual characteristics are crucial for explaining such behavior.

We introduce HALFADO: a lightweight, semi-supervised anomaly detection algorithm designed for data streams. Like many advanced computing techniques, our approach leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to enhance performance. Specifically, it utilizes easily acquired unlabeled stream data to identify suspicious anomalies and then queries these data points for human annotation. Queries are kept minimal to control costs, requiring only that previously flagged suspicious events be examined. Upon receiving feedback, the model updates its prediction rules. When applied to streaming financial transactions, HALFADO successfully identifies fraudulent and suspicious activities with just a small initial dataset of modest volume, while necessitating sparse queries—often characterized as light "peaks" in data volumes—there lightening burdens and reducing costs associated with processing data streams and detecting suspicious activities with the use of automated systems that are simple in design but robust in nature.

Human teachers commonly convey information through speech, written text, and actions; however, incorporating all three to create consistent multimodal data sets for robots remains challenging, particularly when using human instructors who must synchronize their movements with audio and captions. We propose using a collaborative robot as a platform to gather large-scale kinetic description datasets, focusing on everyday object manipulation tasks. To enable efficient training of an end-to-end learning system that fuses image, video, and audio inputs, we introduce a novel embedding approach for reducing dimensionality in non-textual data. Crucially, to characterize physical actions effectively within the audio, we identified three pivotal feature categories—tone of voice speaking speed, and silence intervals—that are essential for describing task dynamics. Finally, we assembled a kinetic description dataset involving 1,000 unique object manipulation tasks across various rooms of a office building, featuring 2,669 recordings of distinct human instructors performing these tasks, which serves to validate our novel non-textual data compression technique.

Few-shot learning is dedicated to categorizing new classes using minimal labeled examples. Despite notable advancements in this field recently, the majority of current methods rely on computing averages for data clustering prototypes and remain hindered by outliers. Addressing this issue, we present a straightforward yet potent framework tailored to few-shot classification. By integrating an episodic prototype generation component, the system successfully creates robust representative profiles from sparse support sets that remain close to the target category and are less susceptible to anomalies. Empirical evaluations confirm that this module not only pushes past previous approaches but achieves significant improvements upon standard models. Specifically, the method delivered competitive and improved results across the *mini*ImageNet, *tiered*ImageNet, and cross-domain (transfer) benchmarks from *mini*ImageNet and CUB-200-2011 datasets.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has gained significant interest from researchers for its potential to mitigate data sparsity in recommender systems. Nevertheless, existing single- or dual-target CDR techniques frequently face limitations, including the requirement that at least one domain contains sufficient data and their strong reliance on domain-invariant preferences. These assumptions are often unrealistic in scenarios where sparsity is widespread, potentially hampering user preference learning. Addressing these challenges, we introduce MSDCR (Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation), an advanced multi-target CDR framework that assumes all relevant domains are sparse and aims to enhance recommendation accuracy simultaneously across each. Our architecture integrates a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preferences Enhancement (GAPE) module; these operate by utilizing the aspectual diversity found in other domains to boost domain-specific preferences. Specifically, GAPE adapts the identification of complementary attributes based on context and transfer mechanisms, while the MDSN employs adversarial training to maintain the unique characteristics of domain-specific preferences alongside the incoming information with other domains, ensuring that domain uniqueness is preserved while complementarity is identified adaptively. Furthermore, we incorporated Multi-Domain Adaptable Neural Networks to extract a user's domain-uninvaritative aspectual preferences. Ultimately, the synthesis of strengthened specific and domain-uninvaritative aspectual tendencies allows MSDCR to achieve a more extensive understanding of user preferences even among sparse datasets compared with single- or bi-target CDR. Rapid increases in MRI datasets, particularly those at large scales, make automated quality control (QC) critical. Although multiple efforts have crafted reliable QC pipelines, generalizing these methods to new, unseen data remains challenging due to inherent biases in MRI information. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline across several large datasets, including ABIDE (N=1,102) and CATI-derived sets (N=9,037), using these same sources for both training and assessment. Our focus centered on MRIQC components responsible for noise estimation, structural similarity index calculations, and outlier detection. Findings indicate that outlier identification using non-domain-adapted models remains robust across diverse cohorts, despite varying pathological inclusion rates. However, both raw and de-noised estimation metrics were poorly generalized. These outcomes suggest highly effective overall QC performance from an system-level perspective, even when specific outlier detectors struggle, notably when training and testing occur within such extensive datasets. Consequently, this approach yields accurate outlying sample identification in major neuroimaging collections like those from CATI and ABIDE.

This paper examines the impact of privately owned electric vehicles on power system stability during disruptions. To capture the decentralized interactions within transportation and energy domains, we introduce a Network-based Multi-Agent Optimization with Equilibrium Constraints (N-MOPEC) framework. Specifically designed for a high-dimensional non-convex problem, our solution employs a specialized algorithm relying on precise convex reformulation. Extensive numerical experiments validate both the proposed methodology's efficacy in visualization and its potential policy ramifications, establishing a robust basis to advance resilience research on integrated transportation-power networks influenced by private EVs.

The analysis reveals that for in-memory workloads, performance degrades progressively and significantly as nonvolatile caches are utilized deeper. In comparison, applications designed for nonvolatile features demonstrate wide variance in performance and exhibit strong scalability when increasing thread counts are deployed. Optane DC PMMs are identified as a unique instance of performance-critical nonvolatile RAM, complementing prior research on the Microsoft ReFS nonvolatile disk and NAND drives due to NVM's differing address space and persistence characteristics. Consequently, performance evaluation must account for both the application and specific NVM usage scenario. To facilitate this, the report presents a framework for assessing NVM-based systems by addressing three key inquiries regarding the storage engine, the application itself, and the NVM utilization strategy.

High angular resolution surveys at millimeter and sub-millimeter wavelengths reveal that disks surrounding infant stars typically display morphology composed of azimuthal or point-symmetric features, sometimes including spiral arms, spurs, crescents, and localized disturbances. While most theoretical efforts aiming to explain these observations rely on planet-containing models—assuming disk substructures arise from disk-planet interaction—confirmed exoplanet detections within these systems remain scarce. Moreover, theoretical expectations indicate that certain structures emerge *prior* to planet formation as they facilitate the accumulation of small solids into planetesimals. Consequently, the authors of this work utilize high-resolution 3D radiative hydrodynamic simulations to predict observational signatures for the evolution of gas and solids in such disks. Narrowed in on substructures in size-grain distributions caused by vertical shear instability among particles at millimeter and sub-millimeter scales, the authors demonstrate their compatibility with existing low-depth gaps observed at these wavelengths. Finally, they offer specific predictions for upcoming high-sensitivity and high-resolution observations using ALMA and the next generation of VLA telescopes.

The nature of the second compact object involved in the GW190814 event—specifically, whether it is supermassive or a low-mass black hole—has remained a point of inquiry until recently, as when Fattoyev and collaborators developed the BigApple energy density functional (EDF). Notably, their initial BigApple iteration predicted a neutron star mass of 2.60 $M_\odot$, a figure that aligns closely with observations from the V645 Herce variable star study. Building on this initial model, a trio of researchers created BigApple-L, an EDF formulation explicitly tailored to satisfy constraints imposed by both nuclear saturation saturation energy and saturation density. In their study, these researchers examined various properties of nuclear ground states using the original BigApple, its revised variant BigApple-L, and the small Apple size categories (sizes A).

This study employs Density Functional Theory (DFT) alongside Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) to analyze the electronic structure of SrMnO$_3$. A pivotal aspect of this methodology lies in defining the correlated subspace and constructing the associated Wannier functions. While SrMnO$_3$, due to its crystal field splitting of Mn-$3d$ orbitals and their clear separation from O-$2$p$ bands, initially suggests that a 3-band $d$-exclusive model suffices, we demonstrate that the calculated spectrum remains significantly sensitive to both the count of correlated orbitals and the bands incorporated into the Wannier function setup. Using the recent real-axis FTPS (Fork Tensor Product State) impurity solver—which offers the required spectral resolution—we show, for instance that a hybrid $d$-$dp$ model yields a split lower Hubbard band exhibiting complex structure unobserved in $d$-only approximations. Furthermore, the spectral features of our 5-band $d$-$dp$ model align well with Photoelectron Spectroscopy (PES) and X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS) data. Finally, these findings confirm that the FTPS solver enables complete 5-band DMFT calculations to be executed directly on the real-frequency axis.

This study presents the design and implementation of frequency-robust Mølmer–Sørensen gates for a linear trapped ion architecture, utilizing Gaussian amplitude modulation coupled with a double-sideband locking strategy. This approach confers resilience against laser tuning inaccuracies by distributing transition probability equally among all possible atom-photon resonance combinations (single, double, etc.). While previous experiments demonstrated that double resonance gates are particularly sensitive to detuning, we found that our combined modulation/detuning method results in a significantly reduced sensitivity to frequency shifts. Specifically, experiments indicated only a 2% variation in fidelity across a 200 MHz range (from -120 to +80 MHz relative to the atomic transition), allowing for the use of less precise, commercially available diode lasers. Additionally, this methodology was verified in a three-ion configuration, producing state-of-the-art fidelity scores of 0.9958 ± 0.0017 for two-qubit logical operations.

By combining multiple many-body methodologies, we investigate potential symmetry-breaking transitions leading to Mott-Hubbard states, orders associated with charge or magnetism, and an unconventional f-wave symmetric superconducting phase specific to this compound.

Accurately reconstructing and dense aligning faces in 3D, especially in uncontrolled settings ("in the wild") where images suffer from occlusion or large head movements, remains a difficult challenge due to missing face details and expanded modeling spaces. The core of our approach lies in modeling occlusion and head pose together, which allows us to split a highly complex task into several more tractable subproblems. These outputs are then synthesized by a self-alignment mechanism designed with awareness of the occlusion topology to produce the ultimate 3D face geometry. Comprehensive evaluations across two major benchmarks—specifically AFLW2000‑3D and FloReCT—confirm that our method significantly exceeds the accuracy of other leading techniques.

Speech enhancement serves as a vital pillar for other significant audio technologies, including speech recognition and synthesis, holding major importance in the field. This study presents a new deep learning framework for this task, which implements a comprehensive attention mechanism integrated with a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence approach to exploit all available latent details following key sampling frames. Expanding upon existing attention-driven recurrent networks, this proposed bidirectional attentional design achieves an improved performance quality regarding the PESQ score, surpassing results from baselines OM-LSA, CNN-LSTM, T-GSA, as well as its unidirectional attentional LSTM counterpart.

Bio-Safety Levels (BSLs) designate Negative Pressure Rooms (NPRs) as a critical necessity for biolabs to contain dangerous bio-aerosols; however, the mechanisms for effectively achieving and verifying negative pressure remain controversial. This paper introduces a control system designed specifically to maintain negative pressure in NPRs by estimating these pressures through flow measurements and adjusting corresponding valve openings. The approach relies on a nonlinear first-principles building model incorporating fluid dynamics to describe airflow patterns. The system's experimental validation was conducted in an NPR located at BSL-2. Results indicate that the control strategy effectively achieves and sustains negative pressure, though it requires calibration using actual airflow data to ensure accuracy.

Storage is vital for providing firm power in decarbonized electric systems. However, retrospective analyses often reveal that storage providers may neglect acting on robust pricing signals during periods of scarcity. Although this phenomenon has traditionally been blamed on forecasting mistakes or operational breakdowns, this paper argues instead that it stems from the strategies employed in risk-averse unit scheduling. By implementing a stochastic self-dispatch model utilizing actual data from Australia’s National Electricity Market, the authors show that storage entities driven by risk concerns adopt a short-sighted approach: these resources prioritize immediate arbitrage and target select extreme price events, consequently choosing to remain offline despite facing significantly volatile market rates at various times. These insights carry crucial policy weight, particularly because calculating the precise level of risk aversion for a given unit remains opaque, complicating judgment regarding market intervention.

Within quantum systems, the evolution of superposition states between electronic configurations occurs on ultrafast scales (ranging from attoseconds to femtoseconds, where one attosecond equals 10$^{-18}$ seconds), resulting in charge densities that vary with time. By utilizing the inaugural attosecond-precision soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser, this study induces a coherent core-hole excitation within nitric oxide molecules. Furthermore, a circularly polarized infrared laser pulse serves as a timing reference ("attoclock"), rendering electron dynamics visible and allowing control over coherent electron motion by adjusting the photon energy of the incident x-ray pulse. Moreover, core-excited states constitute an ideal experimental platform because their intrinsic lifespans span several hundred attoseconds; however, their properties can be optimized to significantly enhance both phase and amplitude. Consequently, this technique paves the path for investigating coherent chemical reactions operating on the attosecond timescale.

We investigated potential regimes of global atmospheric circulation in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified Global Climate Model built upon Hamburg's Universal Atmospheric Model. This simplified framework employed linearized friction in the planetary boundary layer, Newtonian cooling, and processes for dry convection and latent heat release to create a model of circulation. We found that an increase in the planetary rotation rate yields a rise in the number of global jets, with a transition from an earth-like rotation rate (1$\times$) featuring a single jet to slow-rotating scenarios ($\le$0.3$\times$) characterized by a single equatorial supercell. An intermediate rotation rate (0.4$\times$) produced anomalous circulation, generating only broad, circulation-hindering wave structures that failed to develop into distinct high-latitude jets or tripoles. For configurations mimicking Jupiter, Saturn, and earth, increasing the planetary albedo or reducing the planetary albedo had reduced influence on circulation; however, reducing the planetary albedo to produce more extreme climates significantly amplified circulation changes. Our results from the planetary model demonstrate that reducing the planet's radius or slowing its rotation leads to more dramatic reductions in circulation; conversely, chemical changes, such as reducing the planet's magnetic field, have little direct impact on the atmospheric circulation itself.

Active learning (AL) seeks to identify an optimal subset of labeled data, enabling deep neural networks (DNN) to achieve superior performance. In high-cost industrial settings, where every available tool helps mitigate data labeling expenses, AL holds significant potential. The advent of self-supervised pretraining (SSP) underscores the value of leveraging rich stores of unlabeled data, which is particularly abundant in industries. Consequently, there is a clear opportunity for SYSL (self-supervised active learning), which integrates active learning with self-supervised pretraining, to enhance performance on unlabeled image datasets. In this paper, we present SYSL, which combines active learning with self-supervised pretraining. Our work begins by defining a comprehensive framework for SYSL, positing that each iteration must satisfy two criteria: maximizing information gain from newly labeled data and ensuring maximum utility of existing label-free data. Subsequent to this formulation, we introduce two innovative strategies: (1) Adaptation, which refines self-trained capabilities to extract more value from labeled data, and (2) Selection, which identifies the most informative unlabeled samples for labeling. This paper explores fresh analytical and geometric aspects of generalized algebraic multiplicity (χ), which originated in works [7, 5] and was subsequently advanced via [20, 23, 24]. Notably, it uncovers a brand-new relationship between χ and the local intersection index of algebraic varieties—a cornerstone of Algebraic Geometry—thereby granting χ significant geometric significance within the framework of Nonlinear Spectral Theory. We introduce a proposal to simulate bosonic pair production by utilizing large ensembles of long-lived multilevel dipole particles coupled to a sub-dynamically driven optical resonator. Entanglement among these atoms, arising from the swapping of virtual photons via a shared cavity mode, increases rapidly and can be characterizing as Two-Mode Squeezing (TMS) of the effective bosonic variables. Because we establish a correspondence between an effective bosonic description and a spin representation of these dipoles, optical homodyne measurements can effectively simulate simple global rotations and population swaps among the quasi-levels of the artificial atoms. Consequently, when free-evolution dynamics act on this system, they give rise to specific "dark states"—states that are immune to cavity decay due to their anti-bosonic behavior—but which serve as highly entangled resources across multiple degrees of freedom. These dark states remain stable even under conditions of inhomogeneous detuning across the atomic ensemble, especially for systems exhibiting strong spatial dispersion. Lasting for extended intervals determined by the atomic transition frequencies and spatial distributions, these states bridge simulation capabilities with practical quantum networking or enhanced sensing technologies by enabling either direct measurement of multi-qubit states or coupling to neighboring quantum nodes via free-space radiation.

Vehicular Communication (VC) protocols significantly contribute to accident avoidance by facilitating warning transmissions, a benefit that is particularly critical at road intersections due to elevated risks of collisions there. Concurrently, Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) stands as a robust solution for fifth-generation (5G) wireless networks. This paper introduces and analyzes the Adaptive Cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol tailored for vehicular safety messages delivered from one source to two destinations, accounting for interference from other road vehicles whose locations follow a Poison Point Process. Closed-form mathematical expressions were derived to quantify both transmission outage probabilities. Furthermore, a comparison with existing methods demonstrates that the ACN protocol achieves notably lower out-ofage probabilities, especially within congested intersection environments, while also enhancing overall performance with increased user rates; these theoretical outcomes are confirmed through Monte-Carlo simulations.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each base station to schedule uplink and downlink transmission modes independently according to its own traffic load. Unfortunately, this decentralization leads to intercell cross-interference, making the combined problem of power distribution and resource allocation a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a computationally efficient, decentralized framework that decouples the scheduling and power control processes. The proposed method first distributes power across cells in a decentralized manner and subsequently assigns transmission modes using a non-cooperative game to reach a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. Two different payoff calculation methods within the game model explore the impact of cross-interference representations and the associated communication overhead. Simulation studies in an outdoor, high-density small-scale cellular environment demonstrate that these proposed strategies significantly surpass the performance of static TDD systems.

Despite numerous theories, the origin of the Hall anomaly observed in the mixed-state Hall resistivity of type-II superconductors remains unconfirmed by the scientific community. In this study, we performed a quantitative evaluation of magnetotransport data from Zhao et al.'s recent research on BSCCO thin films. This analysis attributes the anomaly to vacancies within a vortex lattice, specifically resulting from magnetic field inhomogeneities at the sample edges or during flux averaging procedures. This model aligns well with experimental outcomes and distinctly contrasts with existing theories involving vortex lattice melting or irreversibility lines. Consequently, our findings suggest that similar analysis based on vortex dynamics could serve as a viable strategy for investigating this class of BSCOC vortex-related anomalies in future endeavors.

We characterize finite-dimensional commuting squares of $C^*$-algebras possessing a normalized trace when they yield a hyperfinite, finite-index $II_1$ subfactor, applying these findings specifically to the index range $[4,9)$. As one major application, numerous $II_1$ subfactors within this interval are demonstrated to be constructively hyperfinite. This study introduces a meta-learning algorithm utilizing ODE-based neural networks that explicitly learn gradient relationships. By equipping optimizers with learned gradients, this method introduces a flexible architecture and an inherent inductive bias tailored to specific tasks, even using the most basic model. Experiments indicate that this Hamiltonian neural network-based optimizer surpasses an LSTM-driven meta-learning baseline on both a synthetic problem and the ReLU-activated MNIST benchmark, while also outperforming standard optimization algorithms on the artificial task.

Enhanced model accuracy alone is insufficient; building trustworthy AI is equally crucial for creating resilient systems in high-stakes fields like healthcare, automotive, and finance. We introduce a hybrid multi-agent framework integrating human and computational agents to address this. In our setup, a checker agent employs an agreement-based methodology that penalizes extreme confidence levels to determine trust scores and rank instances. Simultaneously, an improviser agent uses secure data streams, such as human feedback or augmentation techniques, to retrain the primary model. We tested our approach using three representative agent configurations with classification tasks across several datasets. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in both model performance and confidence calibration compared to baseline methods.

Detecting prohibited objects in x-ray imaging is vital for public safety, a task frequently challenged by objects with uniform coloration and poor texture, often leading to subpar results. To address the paucity of dedicated datasets necessitating few recent studies, this research introduces HiXray, the largest high-quality database for security inspections comprising 102,928 real-world prohibited items across eight categories and meticulously annotated by expert security personnel. Furthermore, to enhance detection accuracy regarding overlapping objects and irrelevant details, we propose a Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM). Inspired by how human vision suppresses noise to focus salient features, LIM functions through two specialized mechanisms: the Bidirectional Propagation (BP) unit drastically reduces noise interference from multiple sources, while the Boundary Activation (BIA) unit highlights critical boundary information. Comprehensive evaluations on both the proposed HiXray and the standardized OPIXray benchmarks confirm that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study concentrates on two pivotal aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing, namely schema linkage and value instantiation. We suggest a column selection auxiliary task designed to enhance the model's encoding proficiency, leveraging explicit learning objectives to refine relevance detection and analysis. Moreover, we develop two distinct value-injection approaches that bridge the gap between current zero-shot semantic parsers—often neglectating database content synthesis—and actual-world applications. These complementary strategies collectively aim to improve performance in linking table/column schemas and populating specific values within SQL queries.

This paper investigates the deployment of differential privacy (DP) within graph-structured environments. It examines various DP formulations applicable both to publishing data and associated statistics, and to conducting machine learning on graph-based information, specifically focusing on graph neural networks (GNNs). A primary difficulty in adapting DP for this domain arises because data points are highly interconnected through complex, nonlinear relationships, which complicates the determination of appropriate privacy budgets and the maintenance of privacy guarantees across the entire lifecycle. Furthermore, there remains a significant scarcity of thoroughly evaluated open-source libraries and end-to-end frameworks dedicated to DP-GD processing and training. To address these unresolved issues, we introduce "PrivGraph": a unified framework streamlining DP-GD data release and GNN training. By leveraging self-joins and self-references within the graph, PrivGraph simplifies the implementation details of DP-GD. Extensive experiments supported by a comprehensive survey of related literature and benchmark datasets demonstrate that models trained via PrivGraph achieve robust privacy safeguards while maintaining competitive performance. The source code for PrivGraph can be accessed at https://github.com/DeepLearningKorea/PrivGraph.

Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the dynamics of quantum many-body systems, which are otherwise computationally expensive. In this paper, utilizing the positive-P phase-space framework, we develop an novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for interacting Bose gases. Unlike current methods like generalized or superfluid hydrodynamics, this framework captures complete quantum dynamics, including non-equilibrium correlations and short-wavelength behaviors. We establish a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic protocol capable of simulating non-equilibrium processes over extended periods by employing approximations for quantum fluctuations. We establish a clear link between this linearized scheme and traditional Bogoliubov methods. Additionally, by investigating correlation structures in a quantum shock wave scenario and contrasting our predictions with established many-body techniques, we illustrate the versatility and superior capabilities of this formalism.

Temporal action detection focuses on identifying the start and end points of actions within a video. While current approaches rely on extreme points—specifically anchors defined by their start and end times—and use prediction offsets to locate these actions, this paper challenges the necessity of such intermediates. Instead, the author proposes a direct, end-to-end model for video temporal action detection that bypasses anchors and offset calculations entirely. Central to this design is an innovative segment sampling strategy that provides numerous candidate time segments at varying durabilities and divisions. By matching only one action clip to each video, regardless of its length, the system avoids the over-parameterization found in existing methods. Furthermore, to address potential information loss during sampling, an auxiliary matching task utilizes multiple action clips to enhance performance without extra overhead. Extensive tests on the ActivityNet v1.1 and Datasets v2.0 show state-of-the-art results, delivering higher F-scores at @0.5 IoU and @@0.7 IoU with even higher improvements.

Long-lasting, highly concentrated structures known as palm tree modes (PTMs) frequently appear within the edge plasma of the JET tokamak. Despite ample observational data regarding their characteristics, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear, largely because existing theories have not accounted for PTMs specifically as carriers of parallel current. This work presents the first experimental confirmation that PTMs sustain significant parallel current flows, utilizing visible, electron cyclotron emission, and magnetic diagnostics including ECCD, NMR, and invasive probes. It is established both experimentally and through numerical verification via the VAlHALL parallel current code, demonstrating that these structures function as electron auroras induced by electron cyclotron emission. Furthermore, it is concluded from the findings that PTMs contribute to the formation of vertical transport barriers observable in the JET device.

This paper investigates collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots traveling at a constant linear velocity within the 2D plane. Collision evasion maneuvers are formulated using the dynamic negative gradients of vortex potential fields (PFs), establishing a reciprocal, cooperative behavior among the agents. The repulsive field depends on the relative position and velocity between robots; incorporating vorticity into its formulation guarantees a free-field environment void of local minima. Crucially, this field engages only when a robot identifies a collision path with obstacles, whether stationary or mobile. Through the analysis of kinaematic-based dynamics in polar coordinates, the authors demonstrate that cooperative agents successfully avoid collisions with both non-cooperating robots (e.g., those moving at a constant velocity) and actively antagonistic robots attempting to collide. Specific conditions regarding PF parameters are derived to ensure universal collision avoidance. Final theoretical findings are validated by experimental outcomes obtained on an actual mobile robot platform.

Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology has recently garnered substantial attention within wireless communications research. These systems comprise passive elements that can tune the phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization of incident signals. These capabilities allow researchers to control and optimize wireless channels for particular signal processing and design requirements, presenting significant promise for radar applications. This paper establishes the theoretical framework for integrating IRS into radar systems to enhance target parameter estimation. We analyze how reflected signals interact with both the target and the transmitter/receiver antennas, accounting for incident signal changes, surface transmission characteristics, and direct path signals (if present). Analytical models for received signal-to-interference plus noise ratios (SINR) for IRS-assisted passive radar are developed. We evaluate performance by comparing different configurations of the reflecting surface, including those with uniform magnitude and non-uniform phase and complex coefficients. We introduce a novel spatial processing technique tailored to maximize estimated parameters in these scenarios. Finally, we present a joint optimization strategy for surface coefficients, indicating that as surface magnitude increases, performance improves until it converges with results from uniform magnitude/non-uniform phase cases. This optimization is especially beneficial when the received power from the reflected path significantly exceeds that of the direct path, assuming negligible noise interference.

Fuzzing serves as a primary technique for uncovering software vulnerabilities, even as evaluating and contrasting the performance of individual fuzzers remains an unresolved challenge. Although mutation analysis has long been considered the definitive standard for assessing test efficacy—detecting synthetic faults that must inherently overlap with the ability to catch genuine bugs—it incurs prohibitively high costs for fuzzing contexts, specifically when evaluating mutations independently. Consequently, we introduce FoMea (Fuzzer-focused Measurement), a heuristic-driven approach that streamlines testing by (1) identifying and revisiting only those programs and focus-areas likely to trigger mutations, and (2) calculating a single score per fuzzer. Empirical results utilizing twelve state-of-the-art fuzzers against six benchmarks demonstrate that FoMea (1) accurately reflects mutations detection rates, and (2) successfully identifies both superior overall performers and relative performance differences among fuzzers. In contrast to traditional mutation-based metrics, FoMea reduces processing time from multiple years to approximately three hours; furthermore, it achieves comparable performance in identifying logical mutates and is readily adaptable for real-world software deployments.

Driven by the success of pretraining in representation learning, numerous continual learning approaches have been developed that operate either as direct adaptations of standard training or as extensions of existing pretrained strategies. While effective, these recent methods typically lock the model weights during training, resulting in relatively slow learning rates. To address the limitations of using frozen parameters, we challenge the assumption that model weights must remain fixed and demonstrate that updating the entire network on small datasets can significantly outperform these recent continuous learning techniques. Specifically, we show that training state-of-the-art pretrained transformers end-to-end without any layer-freezing yields superior performance compared to methods that attempt to adapt pretrained weights. Surprisingly, this straightforward strategy even outperforms standard multi-stage training, often exceeding pretrained models achieved before any fine-tuning. The research indicates two key benefits of this end-to-end approach: enhanced transferability of features and reduced optimization issues arising from alternating pretraining and fine-tuning stages. Building on these insights, we introduce a practical method to further boost performance: training the model in two stages, starting with several frozen pretrained iterations before conducting one stage of end-to-end fine-tuning, which consistently delivers state-of-the-art results with increased training speed. Finally, we apply these findings to the Human Action Recognition task, achieving accurate predictions with minimal video data through the use of efficient video-based pretrained representations.

Approximately ten years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya defined the class of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, where each participant's utility function exhibits $\lambda$-Lipschitz continuity relative to other players' actions. Although they established the existence of $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific parameter settings, they could not determine the computational difficulty of locating such equilibria. This study addresses that gap by presenting an algorithmically query-efficient mapping of broader games into Lipschitz games. Consequently, we prove an exponential query lower bound for any randomized procedure aiming to identify $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player, binary-action, $\lambda$- Lipschitz games, where the exponent scales as $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we propose a broader framework known as "Multi-Lipschitz games," which incorporates player-dependent Lipschitz constants, demonstrate a reduction to regular games, and provide an exponential lower bound for these games too, with the critical upper limit being $\sum_{\epsilon} \frac{\lambda_i}{\epsilon}$ in this scenario.

K-fold Cross Validation is widely adopted for evaluating the effectiveness of machine learning models and handling model selection and parameter adjustment. Nevertheless, the inherent randomized data splits employed during cross validation result in stochastic performance metrics exhibiting considerable variance. This paper reveals the cause: the use of randomized folds induces negative correlation in performance estimates. Estimating the true cause involves understanding how these negative correlations inflate the uncertainty of hyperparameter selection, thereby reducing efficiency in finding optimal parameter sets. To validate our understanding and estimate super-sampling requirements for cross validation under varying conditions accurately enough, the authors developed a new estimator that assesses variance post estimation. Drawing insights from this new variance estimator, we propose Confidence Validated Cross Validation (CV-CVC). Confidence Validated Cross Validation (CV-CVC) determines an appropriately sampled number of data splits considering both inflations due to negative correlations and super-sampling requirements for accurate variance assessment post-est. We have provided examples to support the proposed method and have evaluated its performance in multiple standard benchmarks.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at solving complex problems in audio, vision, and natural language domains; however, developing student models that match current top-tier benchmarks often requires excessive computational costs and extended training periods, including dependence on large pre-trained weights inherent in existing foundational models. Consequently, knowledge-learning architectures utilizing teacher-student frameworks have become essential for efficiently acquiring high performance. Although architecture-driven methods have achieved significant results, they typically rely heavily on extensive, arduous hyperparameter tuning, hindering accessible deployment. To address this, we introduce a parameter-free framework for teacher-student learning that demands no additional adjustments and eliminates specific parameterization concerns. By integrating multiple hybrid strategies, our approach captures both global and local knowledge from the teacher network to initialize and refine student models. Comprehensive evaluations across Vision, Speech Recognition, and Language tasks demonstrate that our method not only surpasses recent state-of-the-art architecture-based techniques but also positions itself as a universal solution capable of benefiting various student systems without configuration changes.

Non-rigid registration stands as a fundamental technique in soft-tissue navigation, specifically within laparoscopic liver surgery. Our work addresses the challenge of mapping a preoperative CT-derived organ model onto the intraoperative surface of the liver, as reconstructed from CT or CAM views. This model alignment is subsequently transferred to the actual intraoperative view by utilizing the geometric relationship between the physical organ and its surface surroundings. The method's core innovation lies in a registration framework grounded in skin-like folding principles, which prioritizes maintaining distance along the organ's longitudinal (long) axes while allowing adaptive folding patterns. Combined with an Isogeometric Boundary Registration (GBT) scheme, these components form a two-stage pipeline: the first refines the matching along the organ's boundary, and the second propagates this result into the interior volume. Scene flow involves predicting three-dimensional motion vectors for specific points within a dynamic three-dimensional environment. While these motion vectors provide significant advantages for subsequent tasks like detecting action types or avoiding collisions, obtaining them via LiDAR or stereo cameras demands significant computational resources and manual labor for precise labeling. To mitigate these annotation obstacles, we offer two solutions: a motion heuristic that delivers scene-wide flow with negligible processing and minimal effort, and a deep learning model for learning flow with reduced annotation dependence. We recognize that low-frequency structural characteristics of point clouds remain consistent even when motions blur these features, prompting our method to learn motion patterns from blurred, motion-affected point clouds. Over the past years, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have led to groundbreaking results in computer vision, audio recognition, and natural language processing—revolutionizing technology from self-driving cars to intelligent assistants. Yet, a major hurdle has been the excessive computational load and long training times required by state-of-the-art models, often demanding massive resources. As an effective solution, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a promising pathway to make ANN achievements more energy-efficient and accessible. We present a user-centric survey focused on practical deep learning with SNNs, beginning with an overview of core concepts and training methods. Finally, we look ahead to key challenges and opportunities for future research in deploying SNNs, aiming to advance the field from theoretical progress to real-world implementation and guide further deep learning innovations with spiking technologies.

We introduce Timeloops, a novel approach for the automatic generation of system call filtering policies aimed at containerized microservices. At runtime, this system learns permissible system calls for programs while avoiding illegal ones, with unique emphasis on filtering redundant system calls to boost performance. Timeloops utilizes an adaptive waiting mechanism to introduce latency, effectively simulating Service Level Agreement (SLA) latencies. Complementing this is an analytical model that identifies and removes redundant system calls by leveraging available and required latency thresholds to ensure application deadlines are met. Timeloops is designed to extend traditional blocking I/O management, enhancing both efficiency and flexibility. When applied to microservices that invoke systems under perceived latency constraints, it avoids the excessive filtering restrictions typical of static analysis and the excessively permissive limits of random-based dynamic techniques. This method maximizes performance gains while maintaining compliance with latency constraints, with evaluation across diverse programs demonstrating that Timeloops surpasses both prior art and baseline strategies in systems invoking I/O operations designed to meet latency thresholds.

Investigating the approximate global $B-L$ (baryon minus lepton number) symmetry in the Standard Model (SM) is theoretically compelling; anomaly constraints necessitate three right-handed neutrinos (RHNs), which are also responsible for the naturally small masses of SM neutrinos via the seesaw mechanism. However, direct detection of this pseudo-Goldstone boson DM is heavily constrained because it elastically interacts very weakly with nucleons via Higgs exchange, thereby largely circumventing the stringent limits from direct detection experimenters. Consequently, we determine viable regions of the parameter space that reproduce the correct Dark Matter abundance, remaining consistent with observations from the Large Hadron Collider and indirect searches by Fermi-LAT and MAGIC.

Full waveform inversion (FWI), which enhances initial subsurface models by contrasting synthetic and observed data, suffers as a nonlinear optimizer that can become stuck at local minima despite its potential for high-resolution imaging. Building on this mathematical foundation using the Lagrangian adjoint-state method, particularly within a time-domain context involving expanded sources, comparisons are established among classic FWI, WRI, and ESI; essentially, the latter two can be treated as generalized formulations with different weights applied to classical FWI. Experiments using both synthetic examples and a North Sea field case demonstrate that this framework effectively reduces misfit functions relative to other methods without relying on expensive third-order solvers or Hamiltonians, achieving better performance in scenarios involving strong scattering and significant noise levels compared to standard FWI.

The sundial, a traditional precursor to mechanical clocks, served as a device for indicating prayer times in classical Islamic lands based largely on the sun’s movement and was subsequently introduced to Indonesia following Islamic acculturation. The evolution of astronomy, technology, art, and architecture in early Indonesian history is partially mirrored by its sundials. Given the scarcity of their coverage in existing literature, these historic sundials necessitate thorough research and documentation. General knowledge regarding Indonesian sundials, including their spatial and chronological data, could be gathered via citizen science projects, thereby simultaneously satisfying research inquiries, promoting public education, and raising scientific literacy about the subject. This article explores the broad model of citizen science and introduces the **Suryakala-Nusantara** project as a proposed application for the study of sundials in Indonesia.

This paper explores integrated data and energy networks incorporating Device-to-Device (D2D) communication operating within an Integrated Data and D2D (Ded2D) framework. This system facilitates base station transmissions of data and energy to respective Information-Urgent (IUs) and Energy-Urgent (EUs) users using an information and energy transfer (TFIET) approach based on time allocation. Additionally, the system allows D2D communications to share the spectrum alongside base station operations. Consequently, the system addresses expanding energy and spectrum requirements in next-gen networks. Nevertheless, D2D-generated interference and wireless path loss can notably impair energy reception among EUs. To mitigate these challenges, the work proposes deploying Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS). Specifically, the objective functions aim to balance the rates of D2D communications and energy harvesting by EU receivers. To resolve the proposed challenges, the work proposes an iterative algorithm based on block coordinate descent. Simulation outcomes indicate superior performance across increased rates in communications and energy harvesting compared to existing schemes.

Although current developments in programmable electrostatic phase plates spark doubts about their utility for certain applications, this study examines various plate designs aimed specifically at rectifying spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). In data-driven approaches to dialogue prediction, generating relevant and appropriate responses hinges on properly encoding users' inputs. Current studies suggest that evaluating generated text via automatic or human metrics is insufficient to gauge the language understanding depth of dialogue models; therefore, we propose a series of probing tasks to specifically test the encoder representations of common architectures in these models. Our experiments reveal that the difficulty of mastering these probes varies even among advanced models and indicate that, unlike Transformers which outperform Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) on text generation metrics, RNNs often surpass Transformers on probe tasks. These findings suggest that RNNs retain task-relevant information more effectively than Transformer architectures.

Ground LiDAR-based place recognition is fundamental to global localization and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) in robotics and autonomous driving systems. This study introduces a novel end-to-end global LiDAR place recognition framework that leverages the powerful scene understanding capabilities of 3D object detection for local feature extraction, ensuring quick in-context prediction speeds. By employing object detection as the localizer, our system can operate without relying on previously mapped areas, allowing it to identify and localize landmarks within a newly explored environment in real-time. Experimental validation in the NuScenes dataset confirms that this proposed global localization scheme significantly outperforms existing methods in large-scale 3D LiDAR place recognition tasks.

At low energy scales, electrons within doped graphene sheets are modeled as massless Dirac fermions. To address this and create speech with superior naturalistic characteristics for paragraphs, this paper presents "Semi-Contextualized Network" (SCN), which integrates multiple contextual modules. Specifically, SCN employs an Adaptive Seamless Connection (ASC) component to bridge the interfaces between deep phoneme synthesis models and contextualizers. This adaptation allows for the preservation of distinct phoneme characteristics while incorporating semantic and acoustic context at the phrase or passage level, effectively mitigating discontinuities. Furthermore, by employing a looping architecture for these speech components, the model exploits both directional contexts—forward and reverse input sequences. Experimental results indicate that the proposed system significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art systems in terms of synthesis quality.

Stars and planets both undergo mass loss via extended wind flows, often regulated by the surrounding magnetosphere created by trapping or channel magnetic fields. While the powerful winds of massive stars result primarily from radiative momentum transferred through spectral lines, the feebleer mass loss in solar and less massive stars stems from thermal expansion triggered by the mechanical heating of a corona. The formation mechanisms diverge between stellar environments, where magnetosphemes form from trapping outgoing winds internally, whereas planetary magnetosphemes are primarily deformed by the external force of stellar winds. Despite these differences, the stresses exerted on both systems frequently trigger magnetic reconnection events, producing diagnostics such as X-ray flares and bursts of radio waves. Consequently, this overview will examine the underlying physics, specifically focusing on the shared principles and unique aspects distinguishing these phenomena for planets and stars respectively.

Sequential neural network models are valuable assets across numerous Natural Language Processing applications, yet their linear architecture prompts critical inquiries: to what degree can they spontaneously master the hierarchical patterns inherent in human language, and which grammatical constructs are within their reach? Adverse weather frequently hinders transportation operations. Current methods for anticipating these conditions typically rely on sensor arrays or in-vehicle cameras, resulting in increased expenses and restricted applicability. To maintain seamless transportation services regardless of weather, there is a critical need for a standardized dataset enabling robust training of deep learning models for end-to-end recognition of various on-road atmospheric conditions. However, no such public set has been available until now. This study introduces the RFS Dataset, the first of its kind, featuring two months of continuous recording during divided and continuous motion in cars and at three fixed outdoor locations. The dataset comprises segments categorized into nine classes representing different weather and driving scenarios including clear days, rain, snow, fog, high/low light levels, dark tunnels, straight roads, and curves. These segments were compiled via manual labeling of an approximately 169 hours of footage from a single, stationary, commercial-grade exposimeter. To validate the practicality of using this material for various operating atmospheres, we implemented a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN). This model was trained on the gathered data to distinguish between weather categories and sub-categories during both divided and continuous vehicle operation.

We introduced a Dual-Path RNN (DPRNN) to enhance speech separation by efficiently handling extremely long time-domain sequences. Its design involves fragmenting long data into smaller segments, processed separately by both intra-chunk and inter-chunk RNN components. This study examines three key aspects of multi-time-scale modeling in audio separation: segmentation strategy, attention weighting between small and large time contexts, and compatibility with different loss functions and training methods. Based on this analytical framework, we propose a simplified dual-path RNN configuration. Experiments conducted on the Microsoft RISC dataset confirm that this new model delivers leading-edge separation quality.

We introduce a novel statistical measure based on the minimal spherical scale required to encompass the halo's total mass in the present epoch, utilizing simulation results relevant to dark matter research. By analyzing scales near one-halo radii—specifically the turn-around radius—we assess cosmological dark models' predictiveness through a statistical lens. This radius marks a critical inflection point on radial halo density profiles, where they transition from steep density declines to smoother background cosmological structures. Due to this distinct feature being clearly identifiable in both observational data and simulations, it functions as an robust indicator of halo mass ranges. Consequently, statistics derived within specified turn-radius spheres provide a reliable methodology for differentiating between various cosmological dark theories.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models offer a dynamic alternative for enhancing the depiction of convection within weather and climate systems. Unlike traditional mass-flux convection schemes, this framework avoids assumptions invalid at current resolutions; however, methods to close the multi-fluid equations for atmospheric conditions remain uncertain. We apply a straightforward single-column model featuring only one rising and one sinking fluid with no sub-filter variability modeling to analyze Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection. Results demonstrate that, using minimal closures, this model correctly predicts heat flux scaling (\(Nu\)) across buoyancy for the forcing range (\(6\) orders across \(Ra\)). These findings indicate that an uncomplicated two-fluid approach can successfully reproduce the principal coherent overturning structures observed in convection.

We examine three independent Jaynes-Cummings systems involving atom pairs where correlations exist between some atoms while the third remains initially uncorrelated. Our investigation focuses on the criteria required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. We determine that creating genuine multipartite entanglement is unattainable if the interaction cavity of an initially uncorrelated atom shares only classical correlations with any other cavity. Furthermore, we observe that if the interaction cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with any other cavity, the resulting atomic states *can* exhibit genuine multipartite entanglement. This non-trivial finding offers a potential method for generating multipartite-entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions and could potentially be implemented using existing experimental setups.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector, positioned among only the two LHC and general-purpose instrumentation facilities at CERN responsible for analyzing outputs of particle collisions, relies heavily on a sophisticated tracking system at its core. Testing these prototype read-out configurations and initial units provided critical hands-on familiarity with the renewed apparatus's functionality. Consequently, this paper discusses both the data collection/analytical procedures and associated software specifications for the calibrating new digital components. Furthermore, it details findings concerning track-hitefficiency statistics as well as distributions showing residuals from expected tracks.

In response, this paper introduces GEN, or online progressive policy improvement by generating any sentence you want. Our method extends generative dialogue models using a simple online feedback-driven optimization process. GEN maintains consistent training alignment between teacher-student models while gradually refining offline generation within the offline dialogues. By generating multiple varied replies online in front of users (in your presence) and using only the single best sentence for each dialogue turn in feedback-driven optimization, we avoid most inefficient discussions during training. Furthermore, our method incurs minimal annotation effort beyond standard datasets, allowing easy expansion to vast datasets. Experimental results reveal that our method outperforms recent state-of-the-art techniques on both SASO and Multiwoozy datasets regarding response quality and linguistic metrics.

Knowledge distillation serves as a proven strategy for expediting deep neural networks, wherein a smaller "student" model mimics the soft probability outputs of a large "teacher" network. Traditionally, this process requires access to both the input training data and the internal parameters of the white-box teacher transfer; however, constraints such as privacy concerns or computational costs in real-world deployments often make these prerequisites unattainable. This work introduces Decision-based Black-Box (DB3) knowledge distillation, a technique that trains a student model by extracting knowledge exclusively from a teacher via decision-making predictions on soft probabilities, eliminating the dependency on training datasets. Initially, we address the scenario where the count of labeling decisions surpasses the number of training samples by optimizing the similarity between the distribution of decision signs over training data and those over label vectors. Subsequently, for cases involving point-wise decision making, we propose a decision-based black-box loss function designed to minimize the distance between the student and teacher decisions at corresponding positions. Extensive evaluations across six classification tasks demonstrate the efficacy of our methods and confirm their robustness against various types of noise in decisions.

In image recognition, edges carry shape-related information distinct from the surface appearance provided by textures. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success, especially in computer vision and medical diagnostics, their mechanisms currently prioritize learning textures over edges. This bias often results in inaccurate boundary definition. Since manual medical segmentation frequently depends on identifying organ boundaries—as seen when delineating the liver by mapping the edge first—there is a clear necessity to explicitly incorporate edge processing into models. To address this gap, we introduce Edge-Gated Convolutional Neural Networks (EG-CNN), a configurable module that extends standard encoder-decoder architectures. It functions by strengthening edge perception within the encoder layer, using dual supervision for precise edge prediction, and integrating this refined edge data into primary outputs via gating mechanisms corresponding to their original weights and magnitudes. Our experimental evaluation across major datasets, specifically the "Brain Tumor Seg" 1.099 version and the "Kidner Tumor Seg" 1.099 version datasets, confirms that EG-CNN enhances segmentation accuracy and overall generalization when integrated into various popular CNN frameworks compared to their conventional counterparts.

MongoDB is widely recognized as a general-purpose, distributed, document-based NoSQL database. It offers transaction support across three distinct deployment configurations: single-document transactions driven by the WiredTiger engine on standalone nodes; multi-document transactions handled within replica sets (comprising primary and secondary nodes); and distributed transactions managed in sharded clusters (composed of multiple replicas sets). A primary issue concerning MongoDB's transactional integrity is identifying precisely which consistency levels each mode ensures—a critical aspect often obscured by the current lack of formal consistency specifications and clear pseudocoding of these protocols within the deployments themselves. This paper formally verifies and defines these MongoDB transaction consistency mechanisms. specifically, we present streamlined pseudocoding based on official manuals for the WiredTiger, RS, and Cluster solutions. Additionally, we demonstrate through formal proofs that WiredTiger, RS, and Cluster each adhere to specific variants of snapshot isolation identified as Strong-SI, RT-SI, and Session-SI, respectively. Finally, we introduce white-box verification techniques dedicated to analyzing these formats.

This study presents a theoretical and numerical analysis of light propagation in periodic parity-time (PT)-symmetric waveguide networks comprising a finite sequence of unit cells. We introduce exact analytical formalisms to describe wave propagation as well as bi-directional reflectionless regimes and the phenomena of coherent perfect absorption and lasing (CPAM) within these finita periodic optical systems. By leveraging generalized parameterized spaces derived from the PT-symmetric transfer matrix, the Lorentz reciprocity theorem, and the non-imaginary Bloch phase, we demonstrate that when a unit cell functions in the PT-broken region or at an exceptional point, propagating modes are invariably supported. Conversely, during the unbroken PT regime, the emergence of propagating modes relies strictly on specific conditions: two distinct modes result if two exceptional points exist in the complex frequency plane, whereas only one mode arises if a single exceptional point is present. Furthermore, we establish the criteria required to achieve bi-directional reflectionless propagation and to tune the exceptional frequency for unit cells that are not themselves in the PT-broken regime. Finally, by employing a two-dimensional generalized lattice potential operating as an effective AP tool, the approach allows the CPAM mode to be engineered into either an even or odd state.

Neural network architectures for point clouds have demonstrated significant success, with widespread adoption in safety-critical domains like autonomous vehicle Lidar recognition systems. Nevertheless, recent studies indicate that these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks, which employ subtle semantic alterations like rotation or tapering to deceive predictions. This paper introduces Transformed Point Cloud (TPC), a smoothing framework designed to deliver strict and scalable robustness guarantees against semantic transformation attacks. The approach first classifies prevalent 3D modifications into additive, composable, and indirectly composable categories—for example, including shearing, rotation, and tapering, respectively—offering generalized certification strategies tailored for each group. Subsequent unique certification protocols address specific semantic transformations and their compositions. Empirical evaluations across various standard transformations reveal that TPC surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, notably increasing certified robustness against twisting along the z-axis by 63.5\%, as measured on a ±20° perturbation. The source code and model files are accessible via https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

This study investigates medium access mechanisms within FMCW radar networks under the premise that all devices operate utilizing identical parameters, including chirp duration, slope, cutoff frequency, and chirps per packet. To counter narrowband interference, we propose and analytically evaluate slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols, establishing throughput metrics to assess protocol efficacy. In the context of ALOHA, interference probability and throughput are examined as dependent functions on various system parameters, revealing anomalies distinct from standard wireless communication; for example, when transmitting multiple chirps per packet, higher throughput may coincide with reduced interference. ForCSMA, aClear Channel Assessment (CCA) procedure is implemented to determine success or failure, requiring successful sensing prior to transmission. Analysis of CCA outcomes, interference likelihood, and throughput indicates that, contrary to traditional wireless networking, the highest attainable transmission attempt rates can optimize throughput in certain FMCW radar environments. Extensive simulations validate the derived analytical results and benchmark the two protocols, demonstrating that CSMA outperforms slotted ALOHA in all realistic network conditions examined.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (TKGC) has emerged as a popular technique for reasoning about event and temporal data graphs, specifically aimed at inferring missing information with precision. Within this area, Tensor Factorization schemes have proven effective at capturing the interactions between entities and relations by addressing static knowledge graph completion problems; this success inspired the development of Time-LowFER—a collection of time-aware, parameter-efficient adaptations of LowFER that incorporate temporal factors. Observing existing weaknesses in representing temporal data within these methods, the authors introduce a model-independent, cycle-aware time encoding framework tailored for representing temporal knowledge. These techniques are applied to develop a novel, advanced temporal factorization method called TeTimeLowFER. Experiments on two public datasets demonstrate that TeTimeLowFER significantly outperforms leading baseline approaches.
